fields.title: The Letter of James
fields.subtitle: Iakōbou, “Of James”
fields.description: The most practical book in the New Testament, written by James, the brother of the Lord, to believers scattered among the nations, and full of the teaching of Jesus: “Be people who carry out the word, not just people who hear it.” Joy in trials and wisdom given to anyone who asks; every good gift coming down from the Father of lights; no favouritism toward the rich; faith that is dead without works, and Abraham and Rahab who showed theirs; the tongue as a small fire that sets a forest ablaze; the wisdom from above; friendship with the world and the grace that is greater; the farmer waiting for the rain; and the prayer of faith, with Elijah as its example. The letter Luther called “an epistle of straw”, and the church has kept as its conscience. In the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Greek given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the letter’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the Letter of James?
qa.answer: The twentieth book of the New Testament, a short letter of practical wisdom addressed “To the twelve tribes scattered among the nations”, most likely Jewish believers in Jesus living outside the land of Israel. In five chapters it speaks about trials, temptation, wealth and poverty, favouritism, faith and works, the tongue, quarrels, pride, patience and prayer. Its constant theme is that true faith shows itself in a changed life: “Be people who carry out the word, not just people who hear it” (1:22).

qa.question: Who wrote the Letter of James, and when?
qa.answer: The writer calls himself “James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ”. From early times the church has identified him as James the brother of Jesus, who became the leader of the church in Jerusalem and was stoned there around AD 62, according to the historian Josephus. If he wrote it, it dates from before his death, possibly from the 40s, which would make it one of the earliest books of the New Testament. Some scholars think a later follower wrote it in his name, pointing to its polished Greek and its slow acceptance by the wider church.

qa.question: Do James and Paul disagree about faith and works?
qa.answer: James writes that “it is by works that a person is justified, and not by faith only” (2:24), while Paul writes that a person is declared righteous by faith apart from works of the law (Romans 3:28), and both cite Abraham. Most Christians have held that they do not contradict each other but answer different questions: Paul denies that anyone can earn God’s favour by keeping the law, while James denies that a faith which produces no love and obedience is real faith at all. As the Reformers put it, faith alone justifies, but the faith that justifies is never alone.

qa.question: Why did Martin Luther call James “an epistle of straw”?
qa.answer: In the preface to his German New Testament of 1522, Luther compared James with the letters he valued most, Romans, Galatians, 1 Peter and the Gospel and First Letter of John, and called it “an epistle of straw” beside them, because he found in it little of Christ and of the gospel of free grace, and thought its words on justification clashed with Paul’s. The phrase was dropped from later editions of the preface, and in his preface to James itself Luther praised it as a good book, because it sets up no human teaching and insists firmly on God’s law.

qa.question: What does James say about the tongue?
qa.answer: Chapter 3 says that the tongue, though small, steers a whole life as a bit steers a horse or a rudder a ship, and that like a spark it can set a forest on fire. People have tamed every kind of animal, but no one can tame the tongue: with it we bless God and curse people made in his likeness. James calls for speech shaped by “the wisdom from above”, which is pure, peaceable, gentle and full of mercy (3:17), and elsewhere urges everyone to be “eager to listen, slow to speak, and slow to anger” (1:19).

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Greek and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Greek beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
Be people who carry out the word, not just people who hear it. Otherwise you are fooling yourselves.

— James 1:22

James is the most practical book in the New Testament. It has no long arguments and no stories, only short, sharp paragraphs about the things that fill an ordinary week: hardship, temptation, money, speech, quarrels, business plans, sickness and prayer. Its hundred and eight verses hold more than fifty commands. And it asks one question over and over, in a dozen forms: does what you believe make any difference to how you live?

It has not always been loved. Martin Luther, in the preface to his German New Testament of 1522, called it “an epistle of straw” beside the great letters of Paul, John and Peter, because he could not find in it the gospel of free grace. Yet the church has read it for nineteen centuries as the conscience of the New Testament, the voice that will not let faith become a matter of words alone.

Who was James?

The letter opens simply: “From James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ.” There were several men named James among Jesus’ first followers. James the son of Zebedee, one of the Twelve, was put to death by Herod Agrippa around AD 44 (Acts 12:2). From early times the church has identified the writer as another James, the brother of the Lord (Mark 6:3; Galatians 1:19).

That James did not believe in his brother during his ministry (John 7:5). But the risen Jesus appeared to him (1 Corinthians 15:7), and he became the leading figure in the church at Jerusalem, who gave the decisive word at the council of Acts 15 and whom Paul counted among its pillars (Galatians 2:9). The Jewish historian Josephus records that he was stoned on the orders of the high priest Ananus around AD 62. Later tradition remembered him as James the Just, a man so often on his knees in prayer that they grew hard like a camel’s.

It is a striking thing that the Lord’s own brother calls himself only “a servant” of him. Many readers, ancient and modern, accept that this James wrote the letter, perhaps in the 40s, which would make it one of the earliest writings in the New Testament, or else in the years before his death. Others think it was written later, by a teacher who wrote in his name and carried on his teaching, noting its polished Greek and its slow acceptance by the wider church. Eusebius, in the fourth century, still listed it among the books that some disputed, though most of the churches used it.

To the twelve tribes

The letter is addressed “To the twelve tribes scattered among the nations”. James writes as a Jewish believer to Jewish believers, most likely congregations of Jesus’ followers living outside the land of Israel. Their meeting place is called, in the Greek, a synagogue (2:2). Their Scripture is the law and the prophets; their examples are Abraham, Rahab, Job and Elijah. Many of them were poor, and they were exploited by rich landowners who dragged them into court and held back the pay of the labourers who mowed their fields.

The letter reads less like Paul’s carefully argued letters than like the wisdom books of the Old Testament, Proverbs above all: short sayings, vivid pictures, blunt commands, and a single theme turned over from many sides. But it is wisdom filled with the teaching of Jesus. Readers have long noticed how close James stands to the Sermon on the Mount. Ask God, and it will be given. The poor are blessed, and heirs of the kingdom. Do not judge. Riches rot and are eaten by moths. Let your yes be yes and your no be no. James names Jesus only twice, but his words are everywhere.

The shape of the letter

  • Chapter 1: trials, wisdom and the word. Joy in testing; asking God for wisdom; temptation and the good gifts of the Father; and the call to do the word, not only to hear it.
  • Chapter 2: faith that works. No favouritism toward the rich; the royal law of love; and faith without works, which is dead.
  • Chapter 3: the tongue and true wisdom. The small fire that sets a forest ablaze, and the wisdom that comes from above.
  • Chapter 4: friendship with God. Quarrels and their source; humility; and the arrogance of planning without God.
  • Chapter 5: patience and prayer. Warning to the rich; waiting for the Lord’s coming; and the prayer of faith.

Trials and the God who gives

James begins where his readers were living, in hardship. His first command is startling:

My brothers and sisters, whenever you find yourselves in trials of every sort, regard it as a reason for great joy, because you know that the testing your faith goes through produces endurance. Let endurance carry its work through to the end, so that you may be mature and whole, with nothing missing.

— James 1:2–4

Joy, not because trials are pleasant, but because God uses them to make people whole. For anyone who cannot see how, there is a simple remedy: ask. God “gives to everyone with an open hand and without scolding”. But temptation, the pull toward evil that trials can bring, never comes from God. It grows from our own desire, which conceives and bears sin, and sin full grown gives birth to death. What comes from God is only good:

Every good act of giving and every perfect gift is from above. It comes down from the Father of the lights in the sky, in whom there is no change, and no shadow cast by turning.

— James 1:17

Hearing and doing

The best of those gifts is the word, by which God has given his people new birth. And the word is meant to be done. Anyone who only hears it, James says, is like a man who glances at his face in a mirror, walks away, and forgets what he looked like. The one who looks closely into “the perfect law of freedom” and stays with it will be blessed in what they do.

He even defines religion, and the definition is disarmingly plain:

To God the Father, religion that is pure and untainted looks like this: going to the help of orphans and widows in their trouble, and keeping yourself unstained by the world.

— James 1:27

Faith without works

Chapter 2 begins in the meeting room. A man walks in with gold rings and fine clothes, and is shown to a good seat; a poor man in dirty clothes is told to stand, or sit on the floor. James is appalled. Has not God chosen the poor to be rich in faith? To show favouritism is to break “the royal law”, which is to love your neighbour as yourself.

Then comes the passage that made Luther uneasy, and that every reader of the New Testament must reckon with. A brother or sister has nothing to wear and nothing to eat, and someone says, “Go in peace; keep warm and eat well,” and gives them nothing. What use is that? “It is the same with faith: if it has no works, it is dead in itself.” Even the demons believe that God is one, and they tremble. Abraham proved his faith when he offered Isaac; Rahab proved hers when she welcomed the messengers. And James concludes:

You see, then, that it is by works that a person is justified, and not by faith only.

— James 2:24

Paul, in Romans, uses the same example of Abraham to make what sounds like the opposite point: “a person is declared righteous by faith, apart from works of the law” (Romans 3:28). Do the two apostles contradict each other? Most Christians, through most of the church’s history, have answered no, though they have explained it in different ways. Paul is fighting the idea that anyone can earn God’s favour; James is fighting the idea that a faith which does nothing is faith at all. Paul’s “works” are the works of the law offered as grounds for acceptance; James’s are the deeds of love that living faith cannot help doing. Paul looks at the root, James at the fruit. The Reformers summed it up in a phrase: faith alone justifies, but the faith that justifies is never alone. Catholic and Orthodox readers hear James as a reminder that faith and love work together in the whole of salvation. All agree with James’s last word on it: “Just as a body with no spirit in it is dead, so faith with no works is dead too.”

The tongue, and wisdom from above

Chapter 3 turns to speech, and James’s pictures come thick and fast. A bit in a horse’s mouth, a rudder on a great ship, a spark in a forest: small things that steer or destroy large ones. People have tamed every kind of animal, “But no human being can tame the tongue.” With the same mouth we bless God and curse those made in his likeness. “My brothers and sisters, it must not be this way.”

Against the earthly wisdom of jealousy and selfish ambition, James sets another:

But the wisdom from above is, first of all, pure. It also makes for peace; it is gentle and willing to yield; it is full of mercy and of good fruits; it plays no favorites, and it is free of pretense.

— James 3:17

Friendship with God

Where do quarrels come from? From desires at war inside us. “You lack, because you do not ask.” James calls his readers “Adulterous people!”, using the prophets’ picture of Israel as God’s unfaithful bride, because “friendship with the world is hostility toward God.” But the grace God gives is greater, and the way back is open:

So place yourselves under God. Stand against the devil, and he will run from you. Draw close to God, and he will draw close to you.

— James 4:7–8

Then James rounds on the merchants making their plans for a year of profit in another city. “You are a puff of vapor, seen for a short time and then gone.” The wiser way is to say, “If the Lord wills, we will live, and we will do this or that.”

Patience and prayer

The last chapter opens with words as fierce as any in the prophets, against the rich who hoarded wealth and cheated their labourers: the cries of the harvesters “have reached the ears of the Lord of Armies.” To the oppressed James says, be patient, like a farmer waiting for the early and late rains, “for the Lord’s coming has drawn near.” Look at the prophets; look at Job.

And the letter ends in prayer. Whoever is suffering should pray; whoever is cheerful should sing. The sick should call the elders of the church to pray over them and anoint them with oil in the name of the Lord. Christians have drawn different practices from these verses: the Catholic and Orthodox churches see in them the sacrament of anointing the sick, and many Protestants, especially in the healing movements of the nineteenth century, took them as a direct promise for today. All can learn from James’s final example, Elijah, “a human being just like us”, whose prayers shut and opened the sky.

How to read James

James can be read in a quarter of an hour, and it is worth reading straight through first, to feel how its themes return: trials and patience at the beginning and end, the rich and the poor, speech, wisdom, prayer. Then read it slowly, a paragraph at a time, as you might read Proverbs, and let each saying ask its question of you. James is not a book to be agreed with. He wants to be obeyed.

About this translation

The text in this edition is the Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Greek and given freely to the public domain. It is printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. A few of its choices in James are worth knowing about before you begin.

“Justified.” In 2:21–25 the translation keeps the familiar word “justified”. It is the same Greek verb that this translation renders “declare righteous” in Romans, so that readers comparing the two can see that Paul and James are using one word, and asking two different questions with it.

“Brothers and sisters.” James calls his readers brothers fifteen times. The translation says “brothers and sisters”, since the whole congregation is meant.

“The Lord of Armies.” In 5:4 James uses the ancient Hebrew title for God, the Lord of Sabaoth, “hosts” in older Bibles. The translation gives its meaning, “the Lord of Armies”, the God who commands the powers of heaven and hears the cry of the unpaid.

A hard verse. James 4:5 is one of the most difficult sentences in the New Testament, and Bibles translate it in very different ways. This translation reads it as speaking of God’s jealous love: “He longs with jealous love for the spirit he caused to live in us.”

For the reasoning behind every sentence of the translation, with the Greek beside it, see the Open Word Bible itself at openwordbible.org.

fields.title: James 1
fields.body_html:
Greeting

From James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ. To the twelve tribes scattered among the nations: greetings.

Trials that test faith

My brothers and sisters, whenever you find yourselves in trials of every sort, regard it as a reason for great joy, because you know that the testing your faith goes through produces endurance. Let endurance carry its work through to the end, so that you may be mature and whole, with nothing missing.

If any of you is short of wisdom, ask God, who gives to everyone with an open hand and without scolding, and it will be given to you. But you must ask in faith, without wavering. Anyone who wavers is like a wave out at sea, driven by the wind and thrown this way and that. Such a person must not expect to receive anything from the Lord. They are of two minds and unsteady in all they do.

The brother or sister of low position should take pride in being lifted high, and the rich person in being brought low, because the rich will pass away like a wild flower. The sun comes up with its burning heat and parches the grass; its flower drops, and all its loveliness is gone. That is how the rich will fade away, even while they are busy with their affairs.

Where temptation comes from

Blessed is anyone who endures through trial. When they have been proved genuine, they will receive the crown of life that God has promised to those who love him. No one who is tempted should say, “God is tempting me.” For God is beyond the reach of evil’s temptation, and he never tempts anyone. Rather, each person is tempted by their own desire, which draws them out and lures them like bait. Desire conceives and bears sin, and sin, once it is full grown, gives birth to death. Do not be fooled, my dear brothers and sisters.

Every good act of giving and every perfect gift is from above. It comes down from the Father of the lights in the sky, in whom there is no change, and no shadow cast by turning. It was his will to give us birth through the word of truth, so that we might be something like the firstfruits among all he has created.

Hearing and doing the word

Be sure of this, my dear brothers and sisters. Every person should be eager to listen, slow to speak, and slow to anger, for human anger does not accomplish the righteousness of God. So take off all that is filthy and the wickedness that overflows, and with a gentle spirit welcome the word rooted in you, which has the power to save your souls.

Be people who carry out the word, not just people who hear it. Otherwise you are fooling yourselves. Anyone who hears the word but does not carry it out is like a man studying his own face in a mirror. He looks himself over, goes away, and at once forgets what he looked like. But whoever looks closely into the perfect law of freedom and stays with it, not hearing and then forgetting but doing the work, will be blessed in what they do.

If anyone thinks they are devout but does not put a bridle on their tongue, they are fooling themselves, and their religion is empty. To God the Father, religion that is pure and untainted looks like this: going to the help of orphans and widows in their trouble, and keeping yourself unstained by the world.

fields.title: James 2
fields.body_html:
Faith and favoritism

My brothers and sisters, you do not hold the faith of our glorious Lord Jesus Christ while you show favoritism, do you? Say a man comes into your assembly with gold rings on his fingers and dressed in splendid clothes, and a poor man comes in too, in dirty clothes. You give your attention to the man in the splendid clothes and tell him, “Take this good seat here,” and you tell the poor man, “Stand,” or, “Sit on the floor down by my footstool.” Have you not drawn distinctions among yourselves and become judges whose reasoning is evil? Listen, my dear brothers and sisters. Has not God chosen those who are poor in the world’s eyes to be rich in faith and to inherit the kingdom he promised to those who love him? But you have dishonored the poor. Is it not the rich who exploit you? Are they not the very ones who drag you into court? Are they not the ones who slander the honorable name that was spoken over you? If you truly carry out the royal law as Scripture puts it, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself,” you do well. But if you show favoritism, you commit sin, and the law convicts you as lawbreakers. For if someone keeps the entire law and yet stumbles at one point, that person has become guilty of breaking all of it. For the one who said, “Do not commit adultery,” also said, “Do not murder.” So if you do not commit adultery but do murder, you have still broken the law. Speak and act as people who are going to be judged by the law of freedom. Judgment will have no mercy on the one who has shown no mercy. Mercy wins out over judgment.

Faith that shows itself in works

What use is it, my brothers and sisters, for someone to claim faith if that person has no works? That faith cannot save the person, can it? Suppose a brother or sister has no proper clothes and not enough food for the day, and one of you tells them, “Go in peace; keep warm and eat well,” but you do not give them what the body needs. What use is that? It is the same with faith: if it has no works, it is dead in itself.

But someone will say, “You have faith, and I have works.” Show me your faith without any works, and I will show you my faith by means of my works. You believe that God is one? Well and good! The demons believe it too, and they tremble. Do you want to be shown, you empty-headed person, that faith without works does no work? Take Abraham our father: was it not by works that he was justified, when he offered up his son Isaac on the altar? You can see that his faith worked together with his works, and his faith reached its goal through those works. So the Scripture came true that says, “Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness,” and he was called God’s friend. You see, then, that it is by works that a person is justified, and not by faith only. In the same way, was not Rahab the prostitute also justified by works when she welcomed the messengers and sent them off by a different road? Just as a body with no spirit in it is dead, so faith with no works is dead too.

fields.title: James 3
fields.body_html:
The power of the tongue

Not many of you should become teachers, my brothers and sisters, for you know that we who teach will be judged more strictly. For all of us stumble in many ways. Anyone who does not stumble in what they say is a perfect person, able to keep the whole body in check as well. When we put bits into the mouths of horses to make them obey us, we steer their whole body as well. Or look at ships. They are so large, and fierce winds drive them, yet a very small rudder turns them wherever the pilot means to go. In the same way the tongue is a small part of the body, yet it boasts of great things.

Look how small a flame can set so large a forest on fire! And the tongue is a fire. It takes its place among the parts of our body as a world of wrongdoing: it stains the whole body, it sets the whole course of life on fire, and it is itself set on fire by hell. Every kind of wild animal and bird, of reptile and creature of the sea, is being tamed and has been tamed by humankind. But no human being can tame the tongue. It is a restless evil, full of deadly poison. With the tongue we bless the Lord and Father, and with it we curse human beings, who have been made in the likeness of God. Blessing and cursing come out of the same mouth. My brothers and sisters, it must not be this way. Does a spring pour out fresh water and bitter water from the same opening? My brothers and sisters, can a fig tree yield olives, or a grapevine yield figs? Nor can a salt spring give fresh water.

The wisdom from above

Who among you is wise and understanding? Let them show it by a good life, by works done in the gentleness that wisdom gives. But if bitter jealousy and selfish ambition fill your hearts, do not boast, and do not lie against the truth. This is not the kind of wisdom that comes down from above; it belongs to the earth, to mere human nature, and to demons. Wherever jealousy and selfish ambition are found, disorder follows, and every kind of evil deed. But the wisdom from above is, first of all, pure. It also makes for peace; it is gentle and willing to yield; it is full of mercy and of good fruits; it plays no favorites, and it is free of pretense. Those who make peace sow their seed in peace, and the fruit it yields is righteousness.

fields.title: James 4
fields.body_html:
Friendship with the world

Where do the wars and the fights among you come from? Do they not come from here, from your pleasures that are at war inside you? You crave, and you do not have. You murder and you envy, and you cannot get what you want. You fight and you wage war. You lack, because you do not ask. And when you do ask, you do not receive, because your asking is wrong: you want to spend what you get on your pleasures. Adulterous people! Do you not know that friendship with the world is hostility toward God? So whoever decides to be a friend of the world is taking a stand as an enemy of God. Or do you suppose that Scripture speaks for nothing when it says, “He longs with jealous love for the spirit he caused to live in us”? But the grace he gives is greater. That is why it says, “God sets himself against the proud, but to the humble he gives grace.” So place yourselves under God. Stand against the devil, and he will run from you. Draw close to God, and he will draw close to you. Wash your hands clean, you sinners, and make your hearts pure, you who are divided in mind. Feel your misery, and mourn and weep. Let your laughter turn to mourning and your joy to gloom. Make yourselves low before the Lord, and he will raise you high.

Do not judge one another

Do not speak against one another, brothers and sisters. Whoever speaks against a brother or sister or passes judgment on a brother or sister speaks against the law and judges the law. And if you judge the law, you are not doing the law; you are judging it. There is one Lawgiver and Judge alone, the one who has power to save and to destroy. But you, who are you to sit in judgment on your neighbor? Listen now, you who say, “Today or tomorrow we will travel to a certain city, stay there a year, run a business, and make a profit.” Yet you do not know what your life will be like tomorrow. You are a puff of vapor, seen for a short time and then gone. What you ought to say instead is this: “If the Lord wills, we will live, and we will do this or that.” But as things are, you boast in your arrogant claims. Every boast of this kind is evil. So when someone knows what is good to do and does not do it, that person sins.

fields.title: James 5
fields.body_html:
A warning to the rich

Listen now, you who are rich: weep and cry out in grief over the miseries that are about to fall on you. Your riches have rotted away, and your clothes have been eaten by moths. Your gold and silver have corroded, and the corrosion on them will stand as evidence against you and will devour your flesh. What you have heaped up in the last days is like fire. Listen! The pay you held back from the laborers who mowed your fields is crying out, and the shouts of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of Armies. Your life on earth has been soft and given over to pleasure. You have fattened your hearts in a day of slaughter. You have condemned and murdered the righteous. Does he not oppose you? So then, brothers and sisters, wait patiently until the Lord comes. Think of the farmer, who waits for the land to yield its precious harvest and is patient over it until the early and late rains have come. You must be patient as well. Make your hearts firm, for the Lord’s coming has drawn near. Stop complaining about one another, brothers and sisters, or you yourselves will be judged. Look: the Judge is already standing at the doors. Brothers and sisters, look to the prophets who spoke in the Lord’s name, and take them as your example of hardship borne with patience. Indeed, we call those who endured blessed. You have heard of Job’s endurance, and you have seen the outcome the Lord gave, for the Lord is rich in compassion and mercy.

Do not swear oaths

Above everything else, my brothers and sisters, do not swear oaths, whether by heaven or by earth or by anything else. When you say yes, let it be a plain yes, and when you say no, a plain no, so that you do not fall under judgment.

Prayer in trouble and sickness

Is any one of you going through hardship? That person should pray. Is anyone in good spirits? That person should sing praises. Is anyone among you ill? That person should call for the elders of the church, and they should pray over the sick person and anoint the sick person with oil in the name of the Lord. The prayer made in faith will save the one who is ill, and the Lord will raise them up. And if they have committed sins, they will be forgiven. So make it your practice to confess your sins to each other and to pray for each other, so that you may be healed. When a righteous person prays, that prayer is at work, and it can do a great deal. Elijah was a human being just like us. He prayed earnestly that it would not rain, and no rain fell on the land for three years and six months. Then he prayed again, and the sky gave rain and the land produced its crops.

Bringing back one who wanders

My brothers and sisters, if one of you wanders away from the truth and someone brings that person back, let the one who does so know this: whoever brings a sinner back from the wrong path will save that sinner’s soul from death and will cover a great number of sins.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
My brothers and sisters, if one of you wanders away from the truth and someone brings that person back, let the one who does so know this: whoever brings a sinner back from the wrong path will save that sinner’s soul from death and will cover a great number of sins.

— James 5:19–20

James ends abruptly. There is no farewell, no greeting to friends, no prayer of blessing. The last word is a charge: if someone wanders, go after them. It is a fitting end for a letter that has spent five chapters refusing to let faith stay in the head. Even its closing sentence is something to do.

The question the letter leaves

The question James leaves is the one he asked at the start: are you a hearer or a doer? It is not a question about how much a person knows. James’s readers knew that God is one; so do the demons. It is a question about the mirror. Having looked into the word and seen yourself, do you walk away and forget, or do you stay with it and let it change what you do with your money, your tongue, your plans and your neighbour in dirty clothes?

That can sound like a heavy demand, and James does not soften it. But it is not a cold one. The God of this letter gives to everyone with an open hand, and from him comes every good and perfect gift. His grace is greater than our divided hearts. “Draw close to God, and he will draw close to you.” The works James asks for are the shape a grateful faith takes, as naturally as a fig tree bears figs.

Where the letter points

It points, first, to the poor. Few books of the Bible speak so plainly about the gap between rich and poor, or side so clearly with the labourer whose pay is held back. True religion, for James, is caring for orphans and widows in their trouble. A church that seats the rich man in the best place has misunderstood its Lord.

It points, second, to patience. Its readers were waiting, as the farmer waits for the rain, for the coming of the Lord. James does not tell them when. He tells them how: steadily, without grumbling, with hearts made firm.

And it points to prayer. The letter that begins with “ask God” ends with the elders at a sickbed, believers confessing to one another, and Elijah on Carmel. For all its talk of works, James knows that the greatest work is often done on one’s knees.

Where to go from here

James has been preached on more for its single sentences than as a whole, and many of those sermons are in this library. A few places to begin:

  • On trials and patience (chapter 1). A. B. Simpson’s The Practical Discipline of Life (1:2), John Wesley’s On Patience (1:4) in Sermons on Several Occasions, and Hannah Whitall Smith’s A Word to the Wavering Ones (1:6) in The God of All Comfort.
  • On hearing and doing (1:22–25). Charles G. Finney’s Self Deceivers, the first of his Lectures to Professing Christians, and Andrew Murray’s A Doer That Worketh Shall Be Blessed in Doing, in Working for God!
  • On grace and humility (chapter 4). Simpson’s God’s Jealous Love, on 4:5, in The Holy Spirit, or Power from on High, Part II; and Murray’s Humility, whose chapter Humility and Exaltation takes up 4:10.
  • On waiting for the Lord (5:7–8). Simpson’s The Practical Hope of the Lord’s Coming.
  • On the prayer of faith (5:13–18). Three sermons on 5:16: Finney’s Prevailing Prayer, A. W. Tozer’s The Praying Church and Simpson’s Practical Prayer; and, on praying for the sick, Andrew Murray’s Divine Healing.
  • On bringing the wanderer back (5:19–20). Charles H. Spurgeon’s Encouragement to Soul-Winners, in The Soul-Winner, and Murray’s The Work of Soul-Saving, in Working for God!
  • On James himself. Eusebius of Caesarea’s The Church History, which tells of James the Just and his death in Jerusalem.

You can also go the other way, from the text to the classics. Every reference to James in this library can be tapped to read the verse, and the Scripture pages gather what the great writers of the church have said about each passage of this letter.

But the best next step is the one James himself would ask for. Choose one sentence from the letter, and do it this week. Then come back for another:

If any of you is short of wisdom, ask God, who gives to everyone with an open hand and without scolding, and it will be given to you.

— James 1:5
